The name alludes to its chronostratigraphic proximity to the extinction event that wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs at the end of the Cretaceous. The highly modified metatarsal that is known from shows an example of convergent evolution, as it is more similar to non-iguanodontian ornithopods than to other styracosternans. Types include Acrocanthosaurus (a meat-eater), Camptosaurus (plant-eater who left 3-toed bird-like tracks), and Pleurocoelus (a plant-eater who made huge 5-toed prints). For years following their discovery (about 1910), the tracks remained a novelty. When Paluxy River ran low, farmers caught catfish stranded in them. File:Camptosaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Camptosaurus is an early member of the iguanodontia - the group of herbivorous dinosaurs that contains the more derived hadrosaurs. It was robust and bipedal, growing to around 6 m in total body length, and weighing approximately 1 t. Camptosaurus had a beaked snout and tightly packed teeth to process its diet of tough vegetation.

File:Caririchnium leonardii (dinosaur tr.ImageDescription: Caririchnium leonardii - dinosaur track from the Cretaceous of Colorado, USA. (replica; public display, Red Rocks Amphitheater visitor center, west of Denver, Colorado, USA) Dinosaur Ridge, Colorado has numerous dinosaur fossils, including bones and tracks. The most common track type at the site is Caririchnium leonardii, which was made by an iguanodontid dinosaur. The large, wide, three-toed print was produced by a hindfoot. Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous rocks are present, tilted during the Laramide Orogeny in the Cenozoic. File:Chakisaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Chakisaurus is a medium-sized elasmarian ornithopod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of what is now Argentina. The genus is known from multiple partial skeletons belonging to individuals of different ages. Elasmaria is a diverse group of basal ornithopods known from the southern hemisphere. Chakisaurus is notable for having a downward curve in the base of its tail, a trait previously only seen in titanosaurs.

File:Coahuilasaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Coahuilasaurus is a large saurolophine hadrosaur that lived about 72 million years ago in the Late Cretaceous of what is now Mexico. Large Hadrosaurs were very common in the northern hemisphere during the Late Cretaceous, and made up the bulk of herbivorous fauna, apparently replacing sauropods which were found almost exclusively in the southern hemisphere at this time. Coahuilasaurus is a kritosaurin, which are known for the large arched nasal formations above their beaks.

File:Comptonatus TD.png.ImageDescription: Comptonatus is an iguanodontid ornithopod dinosaur that lived about 125 million years ago, in the Early Cretaceous of what is now Europe. It was a medium sized herbivore at about 7 m in length, and weighed around 1 t in body mass. Fossilized footprints found near the original specimen indicate that Comptonatus was likely a herding animal. File:Equijubus TD.png.ImageDescription: Equijubus is the most basal hadrosauroid, suggesting that this group of dinosaurs originated in Asia. It was fairly large at 7 m in length, and weighing around 2.5 t. Fossil remains are associated with grass microfossils, implying that it was likely a grazer. These specimens are some of the oldest known grass fossils, and make Equijubus the oldest dinosaur known to eat grass.

File:Emiliasaura TD.png.ImageDescription: Emiliasaura is the earliest known rhabdodontomorph, and the first discovered in South America. File:Gideonmantellia TD.png.ImageDescription: Gideonmantellia is a basal ornithopod dinosaur known from the Early Cretaceous of Spain. The name of the genus honors Gideon Mantell, the describer of Hypsilophodon, which Gideonmantellia was originally thought to be. Like other ornithopods, it was herbivorous, and had a beak at the front of the mouth and teeth in the back, to process the vegetation it ate. Gideonmantellia was bipedal and grew to just over 1 m in length, and 2 kg in body mass.

File:Gongshuilong TD.png.ImageDescription: Gongshuilong is a medium-sized saurolophine hadrosaur reaching approximately 7 m in total body length. It is characterized by the distinct sail-like structure down the length of its tail. Like all hadrosaurs, Gongshuilong had a beak at the front of its snout, and batteries of teeth for processing its herbivorous diet.

File:Gryposaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Gryposaurus monumentensis is a saurolophine hadrosaur from the Late Cretaceous of what is now North America. Typical of hadrosaurs, it was facultatively bipedal, and had batteries of densely packed teeth in the back of its mouth to process its herbivorous diet. Gryposaurus was a large hadrosaur, growing to around 8 m in length, and had a prominent arch rising from its nose. This nasal arch may have been used for species recognition, sexual identification, or possibly even intraspecies combat.

File:Haolong TD.png.ImageDescription: Haolong is an iguanodontian with porcupine-like quills preserved in the fossil specimen. The unique integument raises more questions than answers in ornithopod biology.

File:Hesperonyx TD.png.ImageDescription: Hesperonyx is an iguanodontian ornithopod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic of what is now Portugal. It was a stout bipedal herbivore, relatively small for an iguanodontian at about 3–4 m in length. Based on its arms, it appears to have lacked the ability to switch to quadrupedality seen in more derived members such as the hadrosaurs. Basal iguanodontians from Europe are rare, and the discovery of Hesperonyx is helpful in understanding their evolution and dispersal.

File:Koshisaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Koshisaurus is a basal hadrosauroid from the Kitadani Formation in Japan. It is named for the old Japanese regional name, "Koshi," referring to the Fukui prefecture where the fossil specimens were discovered. The discovery of the genus suggests that hadrosauroids had higher diversity along the eastern margin of Asia in the Early Cretaceous. As a hadrosauroid, Koshisaurus was more derived than iguanodontidae, but more basal than true hadrosaurs.

File:Kryptohadros TD.png.ImageDescription: Kryptohadros is a hadrosauroid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period in what is now Romania. During the Late Cretaceous, Europe was an island archipelago inhabited by a number of known non-hadrosaur hadrosauroids. The discovery of Kryptohadros established a new clade of these dinosaurs, named Telmatosauridae.

Lophorhothon processed tough vegetation with a beak at the front of its snout, backed by tightly packed dental batteries.

File:Malefica TD.png.ImageDescription: Malefica is a hadrosaurid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Texas in the United States. Like other hadrosaurs, Malefica was herbivorous, processing plant matter with their broad beaks and battery of teeth in the back of the mouth. It could grow to around 6 m in length, and weighed about 1 t. The discovery of Malefica helped to understand the distribution of hadrosaurs in Cretaceous North America, as well as evolutionary lineages between basal hadrosaurs and the more derived saurolophids.

File:Mantellisaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Mantellisaurus was originally thought to be a species within the genus Iguanodon, but has since been reclassified. It is smaller and more lightly built than Iguanodon, at about 6 m in length, and weighing around 750 kg. Typical of iguanodontids, Mantellisaurus was facultatively bipedal, meaning it could locomote on all fours, or choose to walk on its hind legs.

File:Obelignathus TD.png.ImageDescription: Obelignathus is a rhabdodontomorph ornithopod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous in what is now France. It was a medium-sized bipedal herbivore, and like all rhabdodontomorphs, it had a beak used for processing vegetation. Obelignathus can be distinguished from other rhabdodontomorphs by its particularly robust jaw.

File:Oblitosaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Oblitosaurus is a genus of ornithopod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic of Spain. Like other ornithopods, it had a short neck and a beak which it used to feed on plants. The thumb claw of Oblitosaurus was adapted into a small conical spur, and it could likely walk quadrupedally or bipedally. It could reach around 7 m in length, making it the largest known European ornithopod of the Jurassic.

File:Hatzegopteryx.png.ImageDescription: The Maastrichtian , Transylvanian giant azhdarchid pterosaur Hatzegopteryx sp. preys on the rhabdodontid iguanodontian Zalmoxes . Because large predatory theropods are unknown on Late Cretaceous Haţeg Island, giant azhdarchids may have played a key role as terrestrial predators in this community.

File:Zalmoxes TD.png.ImageDescription: Zalmoxes is a genus of ornithopod dinosaur named after the Romanian deity Zalmoxis, as a reference to being "resurrected" from its fossil grave. A fairly small, but robust bipedial herbivore, Zalmoxes could grow to about 2.5 m in length and weighed around 45 kg. It had a large triangular head and a beak, suggesting that it most likely had a diet consisting of tough fibrous plants like horsetails and ferns.

File:Paulodon TD.png.ImageDescription: Paulodon is an iguanodontid ornithopod dinosaur that lived in what is now the Iberian peninsula. It was a large, facultatively bipedal herbivore, reaching up to around 9 m in total body length. Originally named as a species of Iguanodon, Paulodon had the characteristic large thumb spike, likely used for defense against predators.

File:Planicoxa TD.png.ImageDescription: Planicoxa is a relatively basal iguanodontian ornithopod dinosaur that lived in the Early Cretaceous of what is now Utah in the United States. It was a bipedal herbivore, using its keratinous beak to process vegetation. Planicoxa was a medium-sized dinosaur at about 4.5 m in length, and weighing approximately 450 kg in total body mass.

File:Plesiolophus TD.png.ImageDescription: Plesiolophus is a lambeosaurine hadrosaur known from the same locality, but an earlier time period than Parasaurolophus. Though it is nearly impossible to know conclusively, Plesiolophus cannot be ruled out as a direct ancestor. Like Parasaurolophus, Plesiolophus would have had a distinct crest protruding backward from its skull.

File:Qianjiangsaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Qianjiangsaurus is a hadrosauroid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of what is now China. While not a true hadrosaur, it exhibits some anatomical similarities that help to show the relationships between its basal relatives and the more derived hadrosaurids of East Asia. Qianjiangsaurus was a fairly large ornithopod, at about 8 m in length. It had a large beak, as well as batteries of teeth in the back of its mouth for processing its herbivorous diet.

File:Talenkauen TD.png.ImageDescription: Talenkauen is a basal iguanodont from the Late Cretaceous of Argentina. It was a small bipedal herbivore with teeth in the tip of its beak, unlike more derived iguanodontians. It grew to around 4.5 m in body length, and weighed about 300 kg. Talenkauen had a proportionally long neck, and a small head for which it is named. Its name references the Tethys Sea, a prehistoric ocean during much of the Mesozoic Era of which the Mediterranean Sea is a remnant. Tethyshadros was relatively small for a hadrosaur, at about 4.5 m in length, and weighing around 500 kg. As a hadrosaur, Tethyshadros was a beaked animal with a hand formed into a fleshy pad and three-toed feet. File:Tietasaura TD.png.ImageDescription: Tietasaura is an elasmarian dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous period of what is now Brazil. Elasmaria is a group of relatively small basal ornithopods known from the Southern Hemisphere. Tietasaura is notable for being the first ornithischian dinosaur named from Brazil. It was a bipedal herbivore, with a long neck and a beak which it used for processing vegetation. Teatasaura was medium-sized for an elasmarian, reaching about 4 m in length.

Like other hadrosaurs, it was a herbivore, processing plant matter with its complex dental batteries.
